<explanation>
1. Project Type & Purpose  
   - This is an open-source, full-stack LLM observability and management platform (Helicone). It comprises:  
     • A collection of frontend apps (Next.js “web” and “bifrost”) for UI, docs, blogs, and playgrounds.  
     • A logging/proxy layer (“worker”) that sits in front of your LLM provider calls.  
     • A backend server (“jawn”) built on Express + Tsoa, exposing REST APIs and ingest endpoints.  
     • Databases: Supabase (Postgres + Auth + RLS), ClickHouse (analytics), Minio (object storage).  
     • Auxiliary services: cron jobs, heartbeat, background workers, and Terraform/Docker orchestration.

2. Architectural Components  
   Draw each of the following as a box or container, grouping related sub-services:  
   a. Client Integrations  
      - Your application code, one-line Helicone integration, or OpenAI/Anthropic/other SDKs.  
   b. Gateway / Proxy Layer (“worker”)  
      - Cloudflare Worker or equivalent. Implements rate-limiting, caching, security, and request/response logging.  
      - Routes requests to real LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, etc.).  
   c. Backend API (“jawn”)  
      - Express/Tsoa server that collects logs, performs authentication/authorization (via Supabase), and provides REST endpoints for UI.  
      - Publishes data to Supabase and ClickHouse, writes large blobs to Minio.  
   d. Databases & Storage  
      - Supabase/Postgres: primary transactional store (API keys, user/org data, relational logs).  
      - ClickHouse: analytics schema optimized for time-series, cost, latency, session queries.  
      - Minio (S3-compatible): raw request/response bodies, attachments.  
      - Message queues (SQS/Kafka) underpin asynchronous ingestion between worker and jawn.  
   e. Frontend Applications  
      - “web” and “bifrost” Next.js apps: UI for sessions, requests, metrics, prompts, docs, blogs, changelog. They consume jawn’s REST APIs and run ClickHouse read-only queries via API.  
   f. Background Services  
      - Cron (helicone-cron), heartbeat (“helicone-heartbeat”), and Supabase functions for scheduled tasks (backfills, cleanup, metrics pushes).

3. Relationships & Data Flows  
   - Arrow 1: Client App → Worker Proxy (“worker”)  
   - Arrow 2: Worker Proxy → LLM Provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, etc.)  
   - Arrow 3: Worker Proxy → Message Queue / Direct HTTP → Jawn Ingestion API  
   - Arrow 4: Jawn → Supabase (Postgres) / ClickHouse (via pipelines) / Minio  
   - Arrow 5: Frontend (Next.js) → Jawn REST API → Supabase for auth/metadata  
   - Arrow 6: Frontend → Jawn REST API → ClickHouse for analytics queries  
   - Arrow 7: Cron / Heartbeat → Jawn API / Databases for housekeeping

4. Architectural Patterns & Principles  
   - Microservices & containerization: each service runs in its own Docker container.  
   - Event-driven ingestion: worker → queue → jawn → databases  
   - CQRS: writes flow into Supabase/ClickHouse; reads by UI come from optimized ClickHouse routes.  
   - Separation of concerns: proxy/gateway layer decouples logging from business logic; backend server focuses on API and persistence; frontend purely rendering and querying.

5. Tailoring the Diagram  
   - For this full-stack platform, draw:  
     • A “Clients” box on the left.  
     • A “Gateway/Worker” layer in front of LLM Providers.  
     • A “Backend/API” box feeding into two database clusters plus object storage.  
     • “Frontend UI” boxes consuming the API and analytic queries.  
     • “Background jobs” attached to the backend and DBs.  
   - Indicate external dependencies (LLM providers, Supabase managed service, ClickHouse cluster, S3/Minio).

6. Diagram Styling Guidelines  
   - Use distinct colors/shapes:  
     • Blue rectangles for services (Worker, Jawn, Frontend, Cron).  
     • Cylinder icons for data stores (Supabase, ClickHouse, Minio).  
     • Cloud icons for external providers.  
   - Label each component clearly (e.g., “Worker Proxy (TypeScript/Cloudflare)”, “Jawn API (Node.js/Express/Tsoa)”).  
   - Use directional arrows with annotated protocols (HTTP, Kafka/SQS, gRPC if any).  
   - Group related components by drawing containers or swimlanes: “Data Ingestion”, “Persistence”, “UI Layer”.

7. Detail & Completeness  
   - Capture every essential piece:  
     • Container/compose orchestration (Docker, Terraform).  
     • DevOps tooling (GitHub Actions, Supabase migrations, ClickHouse migrations).  
     • SDKs & examples (the “examples” folder).  
   - Annotate any integration points: SDK imports, middleware pipelines, custom handlers.

By following these steps and guidelines, your system diagram will accurately reflect Helicone’s distributed, micro-services architecture, data flow, and technology stack—providing a clear blueprint for developers and stakeholders.  
</explanation>
